newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Groups contesting Kuwait's Oct 7 poll.
newsitem.headline: Groups contesting Kuwait's Oct 7 poll.

text.p: Officially there are no Kuwaiti political parties, but some of the 248 candidates running in the October 7 election for 50 parliament seats belong to political groupings.

INDEPENDENTS - The majority of candidates are posing as independents although some are clearly associated with political groupings or have formed alliances with them. Well-known figures are running as independents like former finance minister Jassim al-Kharafi who is a member of one of Kuwait's richest families which has global holdings. Analysts say, if elected, Kharafi would seek the post of parliament speaker, currently held by opposition veteran and pro-democracy leader Ahamd al-Saadoun. Saadoun is also running as an independent although in the 1992 election he enjoyed the support of Islamists.

KUWAIT DEMOCRATIC FORUM (KDF) - A grouping of leftist, pan-Arab nationalists fielding three candidates, including prominent figures Abdullah al-Naibari and Sami al- Munais. KDF member and leading Kuwaiti politician, physician Ahmad al-Khateeb, is not seeking re-election to the parliament which will take the country into the next century, although he says he would continue a play role. KDF won two seats in the 1992 election.

ISLAMIC CONSTITUTIONAL MOVEMENT (ICM) - A well-organised Sunni Islamist group which some politicians say is Kuwait's Moslem Brotherhood organisation. It is fielding four candidates and backing 23 others. ICM favours making Kuwait and its constitution more Islamic. It supports allowing Kuwaiti women to vote. Women cannot vote or run for parliament. ICM won three seats in 1992 with at least a further two MPs supporting it.

ISLAMIC POPULAR MOVEMENT, OR SALAF - This Sunni group has six members officially running and is backing others who support the general political line, which some diplomats see as more fundamentalist than ICM. Salaf, which analysts say now has differences among members, favours Islamic law and values. The group and its main supporters won four seats in 1992.

NATIONAL ISLAMIC COALITION - It ran in 1992 as a Shi'ite Moslem alliance which included fundamentalist figures. This year, some analysts say, splits have appeared, effectively freezing the Coalition as an active political group. Two candidates are clearly linked to the group while other Shi'ites, including liberals, are running as independents. Over 25 percent of the some 700,000 Kuwaitis belong to the Shi'ite sect. There are five Shi'ites in the current parliament including Coalition member Adnan Abdul-Samad.

CONSTITUTIONAL BLOCK - This group represents some Kuwaiti merchant families, traditonally a key force in the country. It is supporting several candidates in this year's election. The Block won one seat in 1992.

TRIBAL - Kuwait's tribes have held primary elections to limit inter-tribe competition on election day. Analysts say tribal candidates could be divided into three main groups -- highly educated liberals who are critical of the government, Islamists who maintain allegiance to the tribe but also identify with Moslem groupings, and a faction that supports the government and enjoys its backing.

No member of the ruling al-Sabah family is running. Whatever the outcome, Kuwait's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah is expected to form a post-election government even if the new parliament is once again dominated by opposition MPs. According to the constitution at least one MP has to join the next cabinet while non-elected ministers become ex-officio members of parliament. The current assembly has 50 elected MPs and 11 non-elected member ministers.
